{"translation_en":"CYRANO:\n  All those, all those, all those\n  That come to me, I’ll toss them to you in a clump,\n  Without arranging them in a bouquet: **I love you**, I’m choking,\n  I love thee, I’m mad, I can bear no more, it’s too much;\n  Your name is in my heart as though inside a little bell,\n  And since I’m always trembling, Roxane,\n  The bell keeps shaking, and the name keeps ringing!\n  Of you, I remember everything; I have loved it all:\n  I know that last year, one day—the twelfth of May—\n  You changed your hairstyle before going out that morning!\n  I have so completely taken your hair for light\n  That, as when one has stared too long at the sun\n  And afterward sees a crimson disk on everything,\n  So, whenever I leave the radiance in which you bathe me,\n  My dazzled gaze casts golden patches everywhere!","larger_context_summary":"In the balcony scene, Cyrano is hidden below while Roxane believes she is hearing Christian, the handsome man she loves. Cyrano has agreed to supply Christian with the eloquence he lacks, but the words draw on Cyrano’s own long-concealed love for his cousin Roxane. After Christian’s inadequate attempts at courtship, Cyrano takes over and abandons polished rhetoric for an apparently spontaneous confession. Roxane therefore receives the speech as evidence of Christian’s spiritual depth, while Cyrano can disclose his true feelings without being recognized as their source. The immediate stake is the success of Christian’s courtship; the wider tragic stake is that Roxane falls in love with a composite identity—Christian’s appearance joined to Cyrano’s voice and inner life.","interpretive_commentary":"The declaration is an exceptionally strong avowal of an enduring inner state: Cyrano’s precise memories, bodily trembling, and imagery of Roxane’s name continually ringing in his heart make the love seem sustained rather than merely rhetorical. Its expressive force comes not just from emotional intensity but from the speech’s representation of involuntary release. He says that the words arrive and are thrown out “in a clump,” then moves from the courteous French vous to the intimate tu amid choking, madness, and repetition. The line does help bring about a change in the relationship as Roxane understands it, yet that courtship consequence is not the same as a performative promise or commitment. The proxy arrangement creates deception about authorship and identity, not about Cyrano’s emotional state: Roxane attributes the confession to Christian, while Cyrano directly and sincerely voices his own love. This split between genuine semantic force and mistaken uptake makes the occurrence especially revealing."}
